title: Cervical Radiculopathy
lead: Model chapter. All later condition chapters follow this layout.
case: Case: A 42-year-old teacher has right neck pain, arm pain to the thumb side for three weeks, and tingling in the thumb and index finger. No trauma, no fever, normal gait, no bladder change. Right wrist extension is 4/5, right brachioradialis reflex is reduced, rotation to the right is limited. Spurling reproduces arm symptoms. Distraction relieves them. Bakody relief is negative.

Working diagnosis: right C6 radiculopathy. Reason: arm-dominant pain, thumb-index sensory change, matching wrist extension weakness and reflex reduction, and a positive Spurling and distraction cluster. This is a working diagnosis, not a confirmed one.

Plan: education, thoracic mobilization if stiff, manual distraction (since it relieved symptoms), chin tuck and scapular setting, neural sliders if tolerated, monitor strength at each visit. Refer if wrist extension weakens or myelopathy signs appear.

differentials.name: Cervical myelopathy
differentials.key: Clumsy hands, gait imbalance, bilateral signs, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign
differentials.next: Urgent medical or spine review. Avoid cervical manipulation and strong end-range loading

differentials.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
differentials.key: Night hand tingling in thumb to ring finger, neck movement does not change symptoms, positive wrist tests

differentials.name: Cubital tunnel
differentials.key: Little and ring finger tingling, elbow flexion aggravates

differentials.name: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
differentials.key: Pain with arm elevation, painful arc, no neurological deficit

differentials.name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
differentials.key: Arm heaviness with overhead use, positional symptoms, variable
differentials.next: Conservative care; refer if vascular signs

differentials.name: Cardiac referred pain
differentials.key: Exertional, sweating, breathlessness, not neck-movement related

differentials.name: Neuralgic amyotrophy
differentials.key: Severe shoulder pain, then rapid weakness

differentials.name: Pancoast tumour
differentials.key: Shoulder and arm pain, Horner signs, weight loss, smoker

qa: Why is a negative Bakody sign not enough to exclude radiculopathy? Because the sign has low sensitivity in published studies, so many true cases are negative. Always judge it with the rest of the findings.
Why check gait and Hoffmann sign in a patient with arm pain? Radiculopathy and myelopathy can coexist or be confused. Cord signs change urgency and what techniques are safe.
Why use the distraction test before choosing traction? A positive response gives a practical reason to try distraction, while a negative response gives no reason to expect benefit.
The patient says neck pain only appears on Spurling, no arm symptoms. Is it positive? No under the criterion used here. Neck pain alone shows local sensitivity, not nerve root irritation.
Wrist extension was 4/5 and is now 3/5 one week later. What do you do? This is a progressive motor deficit. Stop provocative testing, document, and arrange urgent medical review.

fields.Purpose: Check whether foraminal narrowing reproduces the patient's arm symptoms
fields.Action: Step 1: patient actively side-bends to the symptomatic side and extends slightly. Step 2: therapist places hands on top of the head and applies gentle axial compression. Stop at the first symptom.
fields.Instruction: Tell me immediately if the arm symptoms start. We stop at once
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the patient's usual arm symptoms. Neck-only pain is not counted as positive by most descriptions
fields.Supports: Positive supports radiculopathy, mainly as part of a cluster
fields.Negative result: Does not rule it out on its own
fields.Accuracy: . Sensitivity and specificity differ by study and version. Not quoted until sourced
fields.Common errors: Applying heavy force; compressing in full extension immediately; counting neck pain as positive
fields.Next step: If positive with arm symptoms, do not repeat. Go to the distraction test and neurodynamic test
fields.Caution: Do not perform if myelopathy, instability or fracture is suspected

fields.Purpose: Check whether reducing foraminal compression relieves arm symptoms
fields.Patient position: Supine, head supported, symptoms present if possible
fields.Therapist position: At the head end, hands under occiput and chin or mastoid area
fields.Action: Slowly apply upward traction along the neck axis, about gentle to moderate force, hold briefly
fields.Positive: Arm symptoms clearly decrease or disappear
fields.Supports: Positive supports radiculopathy. It also hints that traction may help
fields.Errors: Pulling into neck flexion or extension; jerking; gripping the jaw
fields.Next step: A positive result makes traction or manual distraction worth considering in treatment

tests.name: Upper limb neurodynamic test A (median nerve bias, ULNT1)

fields.Purpose: Check whether stretching the median nerve pathway reproduces arm symptoms
fields.Position: Supine, arm at the side of the bench
fields.Action (sequence matters): 1) Depress shoulder girdle. 2) Abduct shoulder to about 90°. 3) Supinate forearm and extend wrist and fingers. 4) Externally rotate shoulder. 5) Extend elbow gradually to the first symptom. 6) Add contralateral then ipsilateral neck side-bend to differentiate
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the usual symptoms, and change when the neck position changes (structural differentiation)
fields.Negative: No symptom reproduction, or only a stretch feeling that is normal and symmetrical
fields.Supports: Neural mechanosensitivity. It is not specific to the cervical root
fields.Next step: If positive, consider carpal tunnel, pronator syndrome and thoracic outlet as differentials

fields.Action: Patient places the hand of the painful arm on top of the head
fields.Positive: Arm symptoms ease within about a minute
fields.Supports: Reduced root tension, consistent with radiculopathy
fields.Limit: Low sensitivity is reported in the literature

redFlags.Finding: Bilateral limb symptoms, gait change, clumsy hands, Hoffmann or Babinski
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop manual techniques and compression tests; refer

redFlags.Finding: Progressive or severe motor loss (for example grade 3 or below, or worsening day to day)
Bladder or bowel change with limb signs
Trauma with midline tenderness or neurological signs
redFlags.Immediate action: Immobilize; use validated imaging decision rules per local protocol

redFlags.Finding: Fever, weight loss, cancer history, immunosuppression, night pain
Sudden severe headache with dizziness, double vision, speech or swallowing difficulty
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop; do not manipulate; emergency services

manual.name: Manual cervical distraction
manual.why: May reduce arm symptoms in the short term
manual.application: Supine, gentle sustained traction along neck axis, 10 to 15 seconds, repeat a few times
manual.stop: Symptoms spread, dizziness, increased arm pain

manual.name: Thoracic mobilization
manual.why: Reduces stiffness; may help neck and arm pain
manual.application: Prone or sitting, graded central or unilateral glides

manual.name: Neural mobilization (sliders)
manual.finding: Positive neurodynamic test, symptoms mild to moderate
manual.application: Gentle slider movements, avoid provoking strong symptoms
manual.stop: Symptoms last longer than a short time after treatment

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice for a stable, mild case: education plus active exercise, adding manual distraction only if the distraction test relieved symptoms. Evidence for manual therapy in radiculopathy is limited and the effects are mostly short term. Do not claim that manual therapy corrects a disc or realigns bones. Avoid high-velocity manipulation in radiculopathy unless an experienced clinician has screened thoroughly. The risk-benefit balance is debated.
Is it working? Look for reduced arm symptoms, better rotation, and the same-session improvement in a named measure. If there is no change after two to three sessions, change approach.

exercise.Start position and steps: Lying on back, head on thin pillow. Gently nod as if saying yes, hold
exercise.Progress when: Can hold 10 seconds without neck muscle gripping

exercise.Start position and steps: Sitting, draw shoulder blades gently back and down
Sitting, tilt head toward the shoulder as elbow extends, then reverse
Rotation and side-bend within comfortable range
Band rows, wall presses, then overhead loading
exercise.Progress when: Moderate effort, no lasting arm symptoms

exerciseNotes: Symptom rule: neck ache that settles within a short time is acceptable. Arm symptoms moving further down the arm, or new numbness or weakness, means stop and reassess. This dosage is an illustration only. Adjust to symptoms, goals and tolerance.

modalities.name: Mechanical traction
modalities.comment: Consider if distraction test was positive. Evidence is mixed. Not a stand-alone treatment

modalities.name: TENS
modalities.comment: Short-term symptom relief only. Does not change the cause

modalities.name: Therapeutic ultrasound, laser, routine collar
modalities.comment: Weak or conflicting evidence. A soft collar for short periods is sometimes used for comfort, but prolonged use is not advised

pathway: Any emergency red flag? Yes: emergency action. No: go on.
Any myelopathy signs? Yes: urgent spine review. No: go on.

Arm-dominant pain with root-pattern sensory, motor or reflex signs, plus at least some positive cluster tests? Yes: working diagnosis is cervical radiculopathy. No: reconsider the differentials in Section F.
Is the motor deficit mild and stable? Yes: begin conservative care. No (progressive or severe): refer urgently while supporting the patient.

Supports the diagnosis: arm-dominant pain, matching neurological signs, positive cluster. Argues against: no neck movement effect, no neurological signs, bilateral symptoms. Must not miss: myelopathy, cardiac cause, tumour, infection, vascular event.
First visit: screen, examine, explain the likely course. Many people improve over weeks to months, and reassurance helps.
Early phase: reduce irritability with position changes, gentle movement, selected manual techniques, sleep and work posture advice.
Middle phase: add deep neck flexor, scapular and graded strengthening.
